title: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate
body:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a campaign event Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Juneau, Alaska.
                
                    Chloe Anderson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chloe Anderson/AP
    

   
   ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.   
   The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.   Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."   
   Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator. The owner of a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg who had donated to his campaign told The Associated Press that an FBI agent visited the business and wanted to know whether he had been misled by Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. He said he had not and that "Everybody knows who the incumbent is."   Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."   The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.   State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026.
                
                    Haven Daley/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Haven Daley/AP
    

   
   Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said.   
   Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.   The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.   Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."   "To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.   Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are commingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.   They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.   Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.   
   Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael J. Heyman holds a news conference on a criminal investigation related to an alleged scheme to confuse voters by putting a Senate candidate on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent, at the James M. Fitzgerald U.S. Courthouse and Federal Building, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska.
                
                    Lindsey Wasson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Lindsey Wasson/AP
    

   
   Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.   It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.   Trump during a rally late Friday in Florida said Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan should be prosecuted. He noted U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche was in attendance and said, "He's going to make his own decision."   Trump, then addressing Blanche directly, said of decisions regarding the case, "Todd, please make your own," and watched Blanche's response.   Trump added: "OK, he said 'yes.'"   Peltola, at a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, said she is "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." She said she doesn't need any help in winning the race outside of the support of voters.   She was asked before the rally if it was possible that someone on her campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan: "I have no idea," she told KTUU. "I honestly have no idea."   The Times story revealing the potential recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan was based partly on interviews with a former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired before the August primary. Asked about Rios by the station, Peltola said certain people are "gone for a good reason. If I could fire them again, I'd be happy to fire them again."   
   Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.   Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.   
   Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

title: The Healthcare Election: Florida
description: When federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health insurance expired last year, Florida was hit particularly hard. Now, as the election and
body:
When federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health insurance expired last year, Florida was hit particularly hard. Now, as the election and open enrollment coincide, healthcare is a major issue.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  When federal subsidies and Affordable Care Act healthcare plans expired last year, Florida was hit especially hard. This weekend, as open enrollment begins just days before Election Day, Floridians who use the healthcare exchange are learning what their new premiums are. On average, they're going up 10.4%, according to the state's Office of Insurance Regulation. NPR's Maham Javaid went to a competitive congressional district in Florida, spanning from the Gulf Coast to the suburbs of Palm Beach, to find out if rising healthcare insurance costs are moving votes.(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)MAHAM JAVAID, BYLINE: Bordering Naples Beach are palm trees and pastel-colored mansions. Brittany Garcia (ph), a 23-year-old registered nurse, is walking the shore after an overnight shift. Garcia has no health insurance.BRITTANY GARCIA: I would hope that there is some reform soon because I literally have no access to healthcare.JAVAID: She works as a contractor, so Garcia wants to buy insurance on the healthcare marketplace. Those are plans under the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. Premiums are rising as COVID-19-era subsidies have expired. For many like Garcia, healthcare has become unaffordable.GARCIA: I started looking and nothing was available, so I couldn't buy insurance. And to me, that was scary. You know, it made me think maybe I have to go to another country.JAVAID: Garcia has previously voted Republican. Now, without access to insurance, she's not sure how she will vote.GARCIA: This time, I'm just voting with my convictions.JAVAID: The newly redrawn 22nd Congressional District sprawls across south Florida. Made up of rural, urban and suburban areas, it's home to wealthy communities and working-class families. Politically, it swings between red and blue. Northeast of Naples, Collier County is a diverse area, home to immigrants from Haiti, Mexico and Guatemala. This is where Bianca (ph) and her husband live. They've been without insurance since January. That's when her insurance agent called and said...BIANCA: But I do want to let you know that because they're going to take away the subsidy, that it's now going to be this amount of money. And at the time, I think it was, like, doubled or tripled of what we were paying.JAVAID: She's had to pay out of pocket for an emergency visit to the hospital and pneumonia treatment. Bianca asked NPR not to use her full name because political activists in her community have faced harassment for speaking up. She's going to vote for the Democratic nominee, Pia Dandiya, and her reason is healthcare.BIANCA: She is trying to expand the Affordable Care Act, which I think is really important, especially for, like, families like mine and my husband, where we're working 40 hours a week, and we can't afford healthcare.JAVAID: Nice to meet you.ROHIT DANDIYA: Nice to meet you. I'm Pia's father.JAVAID: On the western edge of the district, Dandiya's father welcomes us into her campaign office.R DANDIYA: Here. Come on in. Hello. Pia, are you here?PIA DANDIYA: Hey, Dad.R DANDIYA: They're here.P DANDIYA: Amazing. Come on in.JAVAID: If Democrats were to win back the House, Dandiya says she's going to work on restoring ACA subsidies, expanding funding to Medicaid and lowering drug prices.P DANDIYA: Healthcare is not a blue issue or a red issue. It's a red, white and blue issue. It's something that is impacting all of us.JAVAID: Her Republican opponent, Casey Askar, wants to eliminate the ACA altogether and crack down on fraud to preserve Medicare and Medicaid. His campaign did not reply to interview requests.The district is home to many retirees and veterans who often vote for Republicans. Several of those we spoke to express satisfaction with the healthcare options they already have, including Medicare and private insurance. But Dandiya says the district she's running in doesn't lean either way.R DANDIYA: This district is actually a microcosm of our country's politics, that it is truly purple, and voters are just trying to find a way to make their ends meet.JAVAID: Deep in the Everglades that span the district, besides the swamps, you'll also find sugarcane fields, cattle farms and people picking up their groceries at the Dollar General.(SOUNDBITE OF CAR STARTING)JAVAID: Deanna Johnson (ph) is one of them. The 24-year-old dental hygiene student has been looking for insurance plans on the marketplace.DEANNA JOHNSON: We're kind of in the middle of trying to get health insurance 'cause currently, everything is so high now.JAVAID: She says her family is feeling the affordability crisis. They had to move inland from West Palm Beach when rent got too high. She's hoping things get better in the future.JOHNSON: I hope we get free healthcare like you know, in other countries. They get free healthcare.JAVAID: Johnson is the kind of swing voter candidates will need to win here.JOHNSON: I voted for the red last time, but this time, now I'm thinking about voting blue to get our country back in order.(SOUNDBITE OF CAR STARTING)JAVAID: At an early voting site in the suburb of Sunrise, Brent Harris (ph), a 58-year-old who works in construction, is thinking about...BRENT HARRIS: Democracy, corruption, how people are treated. Then, of course, there's healthcare, immigration. I'm really, really not happy with the way things are.JAVAID: He voted for President Trump in 2016. This year, he's voting for the Democrats. Harris worries about insurance for his family. One of his daughters is on Medicaid, but her 1-month-old daughter is uninsured. Two other adult kids working multiple jobs can't afford insurance. Harris thinks healthcare is a bipartisan problem.HARRIS: But I think working together collectively is hopefully going to be solved.JAVAID: For voters like Harris, in this affordability election, healthcare is just one more way the math has stopped working.Maham Javaid, NPR News, Broward County, Florida.

title: Politics, norms and the DOJ's unprecedented pre-election headlines
description: The Justice Department, contrary to past norms, has stayed in the headlines in the run-up to the midterm election.
body:
The Justice Department, contrary to past norms, has stayed in the headlines in the run-up to the midterm election.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  The U.S. Justice Department has been busy recently filing cases, investigating President Trump's perceived enemies, and filing election-related lawsuits against certain states, as the midterm elections approach. NPR Justice correspondent Ryan Lucas joins us. Ryan, thanks so much for being with us.RYAN LUCAS, BYLINE: Thanks for having me, Scott.SIMON: Has the pace been picking up at DOJ?LUCAS: Well, look, we have certainly seen a flurry of politically charged cases and investigations by the Justice Department over the past month. There was the search by federal agents at the home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, who's one of Trump's fiercest critics in Congress. That search was part of an investigation into possible immigration fraud. We've also seen two former FBI officials charged in connection with the investigations into former President Biden's son, Hunter Biden.And James Comey, the former FBI director, also was charged this month for allegedly leaking sensitive information 10 years ago. That is the third criminal case against Comey in little over a year, if you're keeping track. And last but not least, prosecutors tried and failed just this week to secure a grand jury indictment against a former Trump White House aide who had provided damning testimony to House lawmakers about the January 6 Capitol riot.SIMON: A long list of prominent names of people who've been critical of the president. How unusual is it to see the Justice Department do this so close to an election?LUCAS: It's not normal at all, Scott. In fact, the department has a long-standing practice that has been observed by both Republican and Democratic administrations over the years that the department does not take overt investigative actions in the two months or so before an election, and it doesn't do that so that it avoids even the possibility of being seen as interfering or influencing an election.There's, in fact, even a section in the Justice Department's internal rulebook, so to speak, that says prosecutors and agents can never do anything with the purpose of affecting an election. And critics, including legal experts, department veterans, say the department's recent actions are clear violations. Attorney General Todd Blanche has pushed back on that. Here's what he said when asked about it earlier this month.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TODD BLANCHE: When we have to execute a search warrant or an arrest, if there's a crime that occurs, we take into consideration the purpose and making sure the purpose is proper, which is what the Justice Manual requires, and that's what we did then, and that's what we do in every case.SIMON: Ryan, please tell us about the lawsuits the Justice Department filed in California and Alaska over the elections.LUCAS: Right. So in the California lawsuit, the Justice Department wants the state to set aside any vote by mail ballots associated with a list of 20,000 names that the DOJ says are likely noncitizens until the voters' citizenship has been verified. This week, a federal judge and an appeals court rejected that request, but the Justice Department hasn't backed down in the broader fight over the state's voter rolls because, on Thursday, it sent out grand jury subpoenas to California election officials, and that is seen as a significant escalation on the Justice Department's part.SIMON: And Alaska?LUCAS: Yeah. That's been a wild ride. So this is a lawsuit that President Trump has said he told the Justice Department to file. The department wants the court to delay certification in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses by a small margin. That's because there's another Dan Sullivan on the ballot, and the argument is that having two people with the same name could confuse voters. The state's Supreme Court already ruled that both Sullivans could run.Things seemed to have settled down until a New York Times report this week that said Democrats recruited the second Dan Sullivan to run specifically to siphon votes away from the Republican. The Justice Department revised its lawsuit to include those allegations. Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation. The Justice Department already has a criminal investigation underway, so there's certainly going to be more to come on that front.SIMON: NPR Justice correspondent Ryan Lucas, thanks so much.LUCAS: Thank you.

title: Week in Politics: Trump's Midwest pivot; sharper Democratic messaging
description:
Week in Politics: Trump's Midwest pivot; sharper Democratic messaging 
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
Week in Politics: Trump's Midwest pivot; sharper Democratic messaging 
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6019280/nx-s1-9986683" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      The president heads to the midwest for two rallies he previously said were cancelled. Has his message changed this campaign season and how have Democrats sharpened their messaging?   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  And late last night, a federal judge in California slapped back at the Justice Department with an order that it may not threaten, intimidate or coerce any state or local elections officials or workers over counting ballots. Some confusion this week with President Trump's schedule. He originally planned to wrap up his midterm election campaigning with rallies this weekend in Kansas and Iowa. On Thursday, he announced he wasn't going - instead would do tele-rallies. But now Kansas and Iowa are back on the president's schedule. NPR's Ron Elving joins us. Ron, thanks for being with us.RON ELVING, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.SIMON: Do we know why these weekend rallies were initially scrapped?ELVING: No, not for certain. President Trump said Friday night that his phone blew up after the Iowa, Kansas cancellations. People were very disappointed, and Trump said he did not want to let them down. We do know a lot of the scheduling is being driven by data analysis, but was there something else? One theory is that the cancellations had generated some kind of a buzz that Trump didn't like, suggestions that he was throwing in the towel in those races in those states. And these are two Senate seats now in Republican hands that the party badly needs to hold, especially Kansas, where no Democrat has been elected to the Senate since 1932.SIMON: President spent last month going from one battleground state to another. But he has been campaigning since early September, in that first-ever Republican National Midterm Convention. Has his message changed at all?ELVING: Only here and there at the margins. Mostly it's about the securing of the southern border and various claims about the economy that are at odds with most voters with what most voters, at least, say they are seeing themselves. That includes the tariffs and inflation and surging gas prices and other things Trump says will just go away right after the election. Lately, he's been stressing his case on Democrats cheating. That includes his accusations of noncitizens voting with no evidence beyond a handful of cases.He's seized on a New York Times report we just heard about. Alaska Democrats had been looking for people named Dan Sullivan to get on the ballot against incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. But the printed ballot clearly differentiates between the two Sullivans, makes clear that one of them is the incumbent senator. And the Alaska Supreme Court has already taken a look at this case, and the Alaska ranked-choice system simply allows more than one candidate from a single party.SIMON: Look, we've both learned to be cautious about polls. Right now, it does seem that candidate quality still matters.ELVING: The Democrats have been outspent. They're battling almost limitless resources from Republican donors such as Elon Musk. Multiple sources say that he has spent over $350 million on this cycle overall. So the Democrats hope that voters will still be able to get information and that that information will be about people who could have run for Congress on their lives outside of politics. Many of them did. Those candidates defy the stereotypes of Democrats as being coastal elites. So, for example, in Kansas, where Trump's arriving this weekend, the Democrats' nominee, Adam Hamilton, is an ordained Methodist minister. And in Texas, the Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico, has been studying for a divinity degree at a Presbyterian seminary and is the grandson of a Baptist minister.SIMON: Ron, what are you going to be watching for Tuesday night?ELVING: All the usual things - turn out, of course, who jumps out to an early lead, which races get called early, which look likely to be undecided. And by the way, those undecided may be undecided for days to come. But this year, with all of Trump's threats, I think we'll be watching as well for interference in various forms, both on Election Day and night and in the days to come. And it's not likely to be over on election night or even the next day.SIMON: NPR's Ron Elving. Thanks so much.ELVING: Thank you, Scott.SIMON: And for more of NPR's sharp political analysis, you can check out the 2026 election tab on the NPR app. It's at npr.org/2026election.

title: Virginia and D.C. sue to block construction of Trump arch
description: A mockup of President Donald Trump's pro
body:
A mockup of President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch stands at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall, June 27, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jen Golbeck/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jen Golbeck/AP
    

   
   The commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit on Saturday to block construction on President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch.   The 45-page lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia called the project "flagrantly unlawful," attorneys general Jay Jones of Virginia and Brian Schwalb of the District of Columbia wrote.   
   The lawsuit is the latest legal attempt to stop construction of the 250-foot tall arch whose plans were unveiled by the Trump administration in Oct. 2025.   The attorneys general also allege that construction on the arch, which could begin as soon as next week, will "inflict irreparable harm" on the District and Virginia, including snarling traffic between both areas. The arch would be located between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. It would stand twice the height of the monument honoring America's 16th president.   
   "Both jurisdictions will need to take immediate and costly steps to assess, respond to, and mitigate these harmful effects," they wrote in the lawsuit. "These costs are severe and unrecoverable—particularly because Defendants have refused to take them into account or adequately consult with either jurisdiction during their hurried and preordained process to approve the Arch and start construction."   NPR reached out to both the White House and the Interior Department for comment on the lawsuit on Saturday but has not received a response.   Trump has previously defended plans to build the arch and said it would be a "military complex" to hold weapons and snipers.  The most recent plans for the arch, which will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission, do not include military elements.   U.S. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkin ordered both sides to talk and to agree on a proposed briefing schedule on the motion for a temporary restraining order by Saturday evening.

title: NPR special: 5 takeaways from a year of listening to swing voters
description:
NPR Special: Swing Voters & the Issues That Matter
    
        
                Download
body:
NPR Special: Swing Voters & the Issues That Matter
    
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6008113/nx-s1-9985211" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                People cast ballots on the first day of early voting in New York on Oct. 24.
                
                    Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Every election, there is a crucial sliver of voters who help determine which candidates win.   These are voters who bounce from one side to the other — the rare swing voters.   And all throughout 2026, NPR has had a front-row seat to how these folks think, listening in as voters in different swing states reflect on President Trump, the political issues that matter to them, and who they might vote for going forward.   In this case, these voters supported Joe Biden in 2020 and then swung to backing Trump in 2024.   They all participated in the Swing Voter Project, which hosts online focus groups every month. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR is a partner on the project.   
   So just ahead of Election Day, what have we learned from swing voters this year? Here are five takeaways:   These Biden-to-Trump voters quickly soured on the presidentVoters are able to draw a direct line from Trump's decisions to their feelings about the economyIt's not like Democrats are popular either!There appears to be a convergence among voters on the left and right in support of economic populismThere's broad concern about artificial intelligence and the proliferation of data centers   Click the audio player above to listen to a special, hour-long discussion about these takeaways and the voters.   This special — "Swing voters and the issues that matter" — was edited by Ben Swasey and produced by Lexie Schapitl.

title: Judge orders an inquiry into potential DOJ misconduct in Trump's golf course case
description: Workers remove downed trees from the Eas
body:
Workers remove downed trees from the East Potomac golf course on Monday.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   WASHINGTON, D.C. — A federal judge is launching a formal inquiry into potential misconduct by Trump administration officials in the lawsuit over East Potomac Park, including whether they repeatedly misrepresented the president's plans for the municipal D.C. golf course.   District Judge Ana Reyes ordered Friday's hearing — the third in as many weeks — to seek clarity from government lawyers days after they acknowledged in writing Wednesday that there is a plan to transform the municipal golf course into a championship-level venue, closing it and much of the surrounding park in mid-November.   For months, Justice Department attorneys representing the Interior Department and National Park Service had maintained in court filings and hearings that such a plan was not yet final, despite President Trump's social media statements proclaiming otherwise.   
   Their abrupt confirmation on Wednesday night prompted Reyes to call both sides back into court, just days after she ordered a halt to tree-clearing and major renovations at the park (which the government promptly appealed).   Reyes opened Friday's hearing by quoting the D.C. Bar Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3, which prohibits lawyers from knowingly making or failing to correct false statements to the court. She asked Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., who is leading the government's defense, whether there was anything he would like to correct.   "Not to my knowledge," Woodward said, explaining that he hasn't read every transcript in the case. "We have lots of binders," he said, to which Reyes replied: "I bet you do."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Stanley Woodward, the third-highest ranking official at the Justice Department — pictured in 2023 — clashed repeatedly with Judge Ana Reyes at Friday's hearing.
                
                    Lynne Sladky/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Lynne Sladky/AP
    

   
   Over the next four hours, Reyes grilled Woodward about the timing and status of the administration's renovation plans. She demanded to know whether officials had not been truthful when they told her last Monday that they were not aware of the park closure that Trump had posted about that same morning.   Reyes called the lawyers' claims into doubt for two main reasons.   Government lawyers acknowledged for the first time in their Wednesday filing that the administration is closing the park next month, both for golf course renovations and to address the man-made peninsula's crumbling seawall. And they said in court that they submitted those renovation plans to the National Capital Planning Commission for review on Friday.   
   Under questioning, Woodward told the judge that the submission had been in the works for several weeks. But, as Reyes fired back incredulously, no one from the government mentioned that in the previous hearings, one of which lasted seven hours.   
   "Am I to understand that for weeks someone has been putting pen to paper on a submission to design the golf course … while this litigation was ongoing, while Department of Justice employees were representing to me that there was no plan?" she said.   The hearing ended with Reyes announcing that she would "open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and [Justice Department] attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated applicable ethical rules."   Reyes said that inquiry may be led by a special master, whom she has not yet appointed but described as a judicial officer with "full investigatory powers." Reyes said if the government rejects her special master, she will conduct the inquiry herself.   Reyes stressed that the opening of an investigation does not mean that the court has found or will find evidence that any government lawyers have violated their professional obligations.   But the relatively unusual move suggests that the judge is finished taking the administration at its word, as she said she has done since local historic preservation advocates and golfers first filed suit in February.   The legal fight kicked into high gear earlier this month when the Trump administration cut down hundreds of trees with less than a day's notice. Officials have denied that the tree-clearing was part of a broader plan to renovate the golf course, but Reyes called it a pretext for beginning work without proper approvals. On Friday, she also ordered the government officials to preserve all relevant documents so the "court can conduct an inquiry without the loss of evidence."   
   "Trial lawyers sometimes tell juries, 'Trust but verify,'" Reyes said from the bench on Friday. "For months, the court trusted, but did not verify. No longer."   So there is a plan. The judge wants to know where it came from    On Monday, Reyes extended her ban on further tree removal and required the government to provide 10 days' written notice before closing or irreversibly modifying East Potomac, which the administration quickly appealed.   She issued a blistering 70-page opinion in which she said the case had become about much more than golf.   "Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," Reyes wrote.   
   Within hours of Reyes' ruling, Trump took to social media to double down on his plan to start renovations in November, saying Reyes "has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."   In response, Reyes scheduled Friday's hearing and ordered the government — including Woodward specifically — to "come prepared to state" whether it continues to maintain that there is no final plan, among other details.   But the reply came even sooner, in a Justice Department filing Wednesday night.   Government lawyers said the National Park Service would submit a plan Friday to the National Capital Planning Commission to review "a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events."   And they said they would soon "close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the Golf Course, consistent with the President's directive."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The National Links Trust confirmed it will cease operations at the golf course on or around Nov. 15. But the government says a much bigger swath of the park will close to the public for seawall repairs.
                
                    Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images
    

   
   The filing says the National Park Service entered into a new lease agreement with the National Links Trust — the nonprofit that operates the golf course — on Wednesday.   Under that new agreement, which was confirmed by the National Links Trust, the organization will continue to operate D.C.'s other two municipal golf courses under a 50-year lease, but cease operations at East Potomac "as of close of business on or before November 15."   
   But details of that plan were still hazy in the courtroom on Friday. Reyes spent most of the hearing questioning Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.   At one point, Reyes accused Woodward of "playing games with words" at last week's hearing and said she refused to do so again. Later, when Woodward characterized Trump's Truth Social announcements as a matter of executive privilege, Reyes erupted: "He posted it!"   
   One particularly protracted back-and-forth focused on whether Trump's Truth Social posts announcing the golf course's forthcoming closure constituted "plans."   Woodward said that Trump's posts are similar to executive orders, directing an agency to take an action but not guaranteeing it will actually occur. To that end, he said the course is not currently scheduled to close on Nov. 15, but that the government has filed a "notice of intent" to close it in keeping with the judge's order requiring 10 days' written notice.   He said "we would never violate the court's order," drawing laughs from many of the spectators who filled the courtroom.   What's the deal with the seawall? New claims of danger emerge    The East Potomac closure will extend far beyond the golf course, removing public access to recreational areas and much of the three-mile perimeter loop beloved by runners and cyclists.   The administration says the closure is necessary — regardless of the golf course renovations — "as a result of the deteriorated seawall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River and is a safety hazard in a state of significant disrepair."   Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, said in an official declaration this week that the century-old seawalls have "been compromised" over time. As a result, she said, "large sections of the sidewalk adjacent to the seawall are underwater twice daily" and more often after extreme weather events.   
   All of that has caused voids in the sidewalk and nearby grassy areas, she said, as well as "significant damage to the trees along the seawall." Bowron said the National Park Service has documented the deteriorating conditions in various reports and photographs in recent years, as recently as mid-September.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                An East Potomac park bench sits underwater after a storm in July 2019. The National Park Service says flooding is common due to the man-made park's deteriorating seawall.
                
                    Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Reyes asked repeatedly what specific safety issues the deteriorating seawall posed. Woodward said there were concerns about "people falling into the Potomac [River]" — which made Reyes laugh — but declined to expand beyond the photos in the court filings. The judge agreed that the erosion should be addressed but questioned why the administration officials had not made plans to do so — or even mentioned the topic — at any other point since the lawsuit started.   This week was also the first time that Trump mentioned safety risks associated with the park. His post on Wednesday night focused on the golf course itself, particularly holes in the driving range net.   "Golf balls soar through the holes at high speed and hit unexpecting Golfers — including a White House staffer who was, sadly, hit violently in the chest," Trump wrote. "We will hold the judge, Ana C. Reyes, fully responsible for anybody who is hurt, or killed, on this very dangerous, dilapidated, and unsightly Golf Course."   The Trump administration has made a similar case in its threats to tear down the Kennedy Center — the subject of another heated court battle — if it is not renamed after the president. Its board of directors, packed with presidential appointees, voted in September to close the arts center, citing structural decay that posed safety risks.   
   Woodward said under questioning Friday that the seawall repairs would cost between $150 million and $400 million, but did not answer how much the overall golf course renovations would cost.   On Thursday, Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, sent a letter to House and Senate appropriations leaders asking them to block the Trump administration from using any money for the seawall project in order to advance his golf course renovations.   He proposed language they could attach to year-end spending legislation that would block federal money from redesigning or expanding the golf courses, altering roads, removing healthy trees, constructing new buildings or reshaping the land.   
   "It would be unconscionable to let President Trump direct taxpayers to pay for the most expensive portion of the park's maintenance needs and then take it from them to create a golf course catering to him and his billionaire buddies," Huffman wrote. "Congress must ensure it does not happen."   Congress passed an act designating East Potomac as a public park in 1897, declaring that the land be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." Locals worry the golf course redevelopment would change that.

schema.headline: Judge orders an inquiry into potential DOJ misconduct in Trump's golf course case

title: Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms
description: Voters fill out their ballots at an earl
body:
Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting polling place at Bethel Lutheran Church on October 28, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minn.
                
                    Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      Ahead of Election Day, there are a lot of questions about what might happen, what the implications of different outcomes might be and even what it's like to cover elections. In collaboration with the NPR Politics Podcast, listeners sent in their questions about the election and politics for our political correspondents to answer.   Many political polls have been wrong recently. How can you as a reporter provide an accurate news piece utilizing poll results?   This is a common question every election cycle, but it's a little like saying, "I don't like the media because the media is biased." There are good polls and bad polls just like there are good reporters and bad reporters.   
   There have no doubt been some high-profile misses, particularly at the state level. National polls have actually been pretty good when it comes to the horse race, with a slight underestimation of Republican turnout. But remember, these polls have margins of error. That means a poll with +/- 3 or 4 percentage points is actually a range of 6 to 8 points. That's important because in a country with very close elections, the kind of precision that Americans expect sets up the polls for failure because they're not intended to be that specific. They set more of a fuzzy range.   State surveys have seen a lot of junk polls, even a couple fake ones this time around. So it's really important to pay attention to the quality of the pollster. The reason for this is because of the decline of local journalism. Local newspapers and TV stations just don't have the kind of money that national outlets do to pay for good, rigorous and frequent polling.   Horse-race polling isn't even the best use of polling. I talk a lot about polls, but you rarely hear me talking about specific margins between candidates, unless there's been a trend moving the needle in a certain direction. The races are close, within margin of error in many places, and that's all that really needs to be conveyed. Unfortunately, some outlets emphasize the horse race, but the best stuff is underneath. Are there trends over time with statistically significant movement on important questions and issues? For example, we wouldn't know how quickly public opinion moved on important issues, approval ratings, attitudes and how strongly people feel about those things without this data.   
   Also, for those who don't think reporters should use polls at all, understand that campaigns and corporations spend millions of dollars on polling to inform where they spend money, where they travel and what messages to use. They use the same pollsters you hear about externally. All that said, polling is one tool. It's not everything, and it should be mixed with historical context, reporting with campaigns, and being on the ground, which are all priorities of NPR's as well. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent   Do you prefer reporting on midterms or presidential election years? Are there unique opportunities that midterms have?   Presidential elections are certainly easier to cover in the sense that there are two sides who are looking to be in one job. Plus, regular people are very interested in presidential elections, as is evident by the decline in turnout from presidentials to midterms. But midterm elections are also consequential — and can be a lot of fun.    You get a lot of quirky candidates in down-ballot races sometimes with interesting storylines that might not see a lot of daylight in a presidential election, which is like a solar eclipse. Plus, I got my start covering midterm elections, researching the 2006 elections and learning about every single congressional race, and it was fascinating — the characters, the different types of places and economies and people in this very large country. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent   Reporting during the midterms is so much more fun! Rallies for presidential candidates have tons of security and stadium-size venues. A lot of sitting and waiting, using your camera zoom and being stuck in a press pen.   
   Tagging along with a candidate for House or Senate, especially early in the cycle, can be so much more intimate. This year, I've covered candidates at an antique shop, a farmer's market, a UAW picnic, a family farm and a smokejumper-themed brewery. There is more opportunity to see candidates up close, watch them interact with voters and even ask them questions. - Sam Gringlas, NPR congressional reporter   I personally like all elections, which is what makes a presidential year so great, you get a whole smorgasbord of contests. The top of the ticket certainly consumes a lot of oxygen but I've found you can often learn more about how the election is going by spending time with congressional candidates or even candidates for the state legislature. And, unlike midterm years, more voters are engaged, which makes for better voter interviews. But, please check back in a week and a half to see how my sleep debt is doing and whether I still say I "like all elections," because this may just be the light at the end of the tunnel pre-election euphoria speaking. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent   
   Is there a race you're watching out of your own curiosity that may not "matter" at the national level?   Every race counts when it comes to the balance of power in the House and the Senate. But I have been joking that following the twists and turns in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District is now my hobby. I did a story about this race about a month ago and it has only gotten more wild since. It is a district that President Trump won by 14 points that hasn't been represented by a Democrat in its more than 40 years in existence. But Republicans ended up nominating a Trump-backed candidate with a ton of baggage who only moved to the district to run for congress. In an interview with me, he blamed his grandkids for one of his missteps.    Democrats nominated a former Miss Nevada turned state legislator, who has been running a very solid campaign. The retiring Republican congressman is using colorful language to trash the GOP nominee every chance he gets and announced that he voted for a Libertarian instead. So, it's just totally messy. The Republican is still favored to win but I am watching closely because I just want to know how this drama ends. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent   There are a lot of redistricting ballot measures before voters. In Maryland, voters are going to consider whether to [amend the state constitution which would ultimately] allow Democrats to add one more seat there. That one actually looks like it might not pass, which is surprising because this is a Democratic state. You'd think Democrats want to give their Democratic lawmakers an edge to create a new seat.     Coloradans are considering a ballot measure that would basically make it harder for their legislature to mid-decade redistrict, which a lot of other states did. And then in Missouri, they're going to be weighing another question about whether to allow congressional redistricting that would help Republicans flip a seat there.    
   Then there's Alaska. Every cycle they go back and forth about this primary system that they have and ranked choice voting. It is going before them again. It's always a squeaker. It's always really close. But voters have stood by their top four primary nonpartisan primary system and their ranked choice voting. - Ashley Lopez, NPR political correspondent   I'm paying very close attention to places like Michigan and Texas and what they tell us about the Senate. There's a couple of really interesting House races that I think are going to tell us something, especially in South Florida and South Texas with Latinos and how they move in this election, because they're quite the swing group at this point. There are a couple of governors' races and ballot initiatives across the country.    In California, I'm really interested to see how this wealth tax ballot initiative does. There's been a ton of money, tens of millions of dollars spent on that, and it's going to be interesting to see if in a place like California that do tend to be the ones out front on a lot of these kinds of experiments, if it winds up passing or not.    I'm also curious about something like the Nevada governor's race. And Nevada is always a really interesting place because people have a real independent streak. You've got two candidates here in Gov. Joe Lombardo, the Republican who was elected in 2022, and he's going against the state's attorney general, Aaron Ford. There's been all this talk about crime and about Trump and the high unemployment rate. But then you dig into some of their backgrounds. Ford has had to talk about how, as a college kid, he made some bad decisions, including running into trouble with the law. I think the outcome there is going to be really interesting to see, asking voters whether they're going to take the dirt of what happened with somebody a decade or so ago versus the national political climate. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent   
   How is the executive branch going to be affected if Democrats take one or both houses of Congress in the midterms?   Midterms tend to be a check on the party that holds the White House. The way that happens, first and foremost, is when there's split power in Washington, legislation comes to a standstill unless there's compromise and with only about 10% of congressional districts being competitive, there isn't much incentive to meet in the middle.    Some issues that have bipartisan support, like guardrails for artificial intelligence, could see progress. But the president is not in favor of restrictions on AI. The biggest effect of a Democratic House or Senate will be investigations and oversight of the current administration. One thing that could be politically tricky for Democrats is how far they go with impeachments, if they go there. Republicans paid the political price for their impeachment investigations of former President Clinton in the late 90s.    
   Only twice since World War II has the president's party picked up seats in a midterm — once in 2002 after 9/11 and the preceding midterm in 1998. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent   Are political debates dead? And if not, when they are held, are they doomed to be ever more divisive at the expense of platforming policies as they have been in recent years?   In midterms, you have incumbents who are reluctant to get on a debate stage because they don't want to give a challenger oxygen and raise their profiles. The thing about debates is that sometimes people don't feel like they get a lot out of them, because politicians are talking-point machines. The job of journalists and interviewers is to try and get them off of those and to press on vulnerabilities so voters get a clearer understanding of what those candidates want to do and why they want to do it.   
   That's a real service to voters when done well, considering the only things voters see or hear from politicians otherwise is pre-packaged campaign ads, speeches or curated social media clips. Pressing them on their policies in a debate is an important part of the Democratic process, and a big platform for people who need to increase their name identification, so, no, I don't think debates are dead. In fact, I think with what could be a record number of candidates in this upcoming presidential election, you're gonna see a lot of debates. Just wait. – Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent.   
   What from this year's midterms are you watching as potential indicators for the presidential election in 2028?   Jon Ossoff's margin in Georgia. LOL. Ossoff has emerged as a dark-horse potential presidential candidate, despite his denials. They always deny they're running until they do. There are a handful of potential 2028 Democratic candidates who are governors running states where they are heavily favored to win reelection, people like J.B. Pritzker in Illinois, Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, Wes Moore in Maryland. What do they say on Election Night to give any clues about what they do next. Or will they simply say how proud they are of their records running their states, which, by the way, can be hints of messages for… 2028.    
   There will be lots to learn from how Democrats affiliated with democratic socialism or the very progressive wing of the party perform on election night compared to moderates in various places. That could set the stage for the issue debates in the 2028 Democratic primary. Also, how do Republicans run post-Trump? Do any start to distance themselves in the days and weeks following the midterms, trying to lay out a different direction, while walking the line to keep MAGA on board?   You can't really read into how states go in midterms to say whether they're going to be competitive in 2028. These are just very different electorates than much-higher turnout presidential elections. The margin for the Senate will be interesting for 2028 and what it means for the potential of a governing majority for the next president. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent   Thank you to Courtney, Nathaneal, Chad, Erin, Renata and Tyson for the questions.

schema.headline: Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms
